title: Show me your glory (Exodus 33:12–23)
hookLine: Moses in the cleft of the rock sees only God's back as he passes

lines: A WARM CHAIR, A SWINGING COAT.
cards: Have you ever walked into a room just after someone left it? The chair is still warm. A coat still swings on its hook.
You missed them by a minute, but the room still tells you who was here. After the calf, after the broken tablets, Moses has been pleading for his people. Then he asks for something bold.
Not a sign. Not a plan. In the King James Bible: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory."

teach.b: God says yes, and no. Yes: I will make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll proclaim my name. But no: "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live."
So God makes a plan, tender and almost playful. There is a place by me, on a rock.

teach.h: A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.
teach.b: I'll put you in a cleft of the rock, and cover you with my hand while I pass by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen." Moses gets to see where God has just been.
The glory he asked for is kavod in Hebrew. Lexicons link it to a root meaning heavy, so some readers hear glory as weight: what makes God weighty, real, present.
And Moses can bear it only from behind, after it has passed. Readers notice a puzzle. A few verses earlier, the same chapter says God spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.
Some interpreters say the first means closeness, the way friends talk, and the second the full sight of God, which no one could bear. The text keeps both.

teach.h: YOU SEE HIS BACK BY FOLLOWING.
teach.b: Gregory of Nyssa, a Greek bishop and writer, read it as a picture of following God: you see God's back because you are walking behind him.

teach.h: THOU SHALT SEE MY BACK PARTS.
teach.b: The Gospel of John holds both sides too: of Jesus, "we beheld his glory," and a few verses on, "No man hath seen God at any time."
Some Christians say faith is often like this: not seeing God's face, but noticing, a little late, that someone was just here.

how: Some Christians turn to this passage when talking about knowing God in hindsight, and some spiritual traditions, like the daily examen, look back over the day for where God was present.

games.q: you're Moses. you've just asked to see God's glory, and God says no one can see his face and live. what happens next?
o: you're sent back down the mountain.
God hides you in a rock and passes by.
God shows you a vision in a dream.
games.why: God puts Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and lets him see his back as he passes. a no that turns into a gentler yes.

practice: Go back over the last day or two slowly, like walking back through rooms, and look for where God has just been, or, if that language isn't yours, where goodness has just passed: a moment kinder than you expected, a worry that quietly didn't happen.
Don't rush to explain it; just notice the warm chair. If you pray, you can say thank you for what passed by.

carryVoice: Your line: his back, passing by. Seen a little late is still seen. That's day three hundred ninety-eight.
